content: The Creeping Buttercup, scientifically known as Ranunculus repens, is a flowering plant belonging to the Buttercup family. It is native to Europe and the Pacific Northwest. This plant is characterized by its bright yellow flowers and stolons, which are horizontal stems that produce roots and new plants at their nodes. The leaves of the Creeping Buttercup are dark green, three-lobed, and often display white spots. These leaves emerge from the nodes, as do the hairy stems. One distinguishing feature of the Creeping Buttercup is its flowers, which are typically larger than those of many other species in the Ranunculus genus. However, under suboptimal conditions, the flowers may be as small as 10 millimeters in diameter. The plant is also notable for its low-lying growth habit and the presence of stolons. The Creeping Buttercup was originally sold as an ornamental flower in various parts of the world but has since become an invasive species in many regions. It thrives in fields and pastures, particularly in wet soil conditions. Like most buttercups, Ranunculus repens is toxic. However, the toxic compounds are neutralized when the plant is dried, such as in hay. The plant has an acrid taste, which deters cattle from consuming it. This avoidance allows the Creeping Buttercup to exploit the surrounding cropped ground, spreading its stolons further. Additionally, the plant can spread through the transportation of hay. Direct contact with the sap of the Creeping Buttercup can cause irritation to the skin and mucous membranes.
